scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses the antiderivative of 1/(1+x²), which is arctan(x) — a standard derivative rule (Unit 2, topic 2.7 extended to inverse trig, or Unit 3 topic 3.4 for inverse-trig derivatives). The definite integral evaluation uses the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Unit 6, topic 6.7). Both are core AB/BC content with no BC-only or excluded-content flags.

criterion_units.evidence: Recognizing that d/dx[arctan(x)] = 1/(1+x²) requires knowledge of inverse-trig derivatives (Unit 3, topic 3.4: 'Differentiating Inverse Trigonometric Functions'). The CED's EK FUN-3.D.1 lists arctan as one of the standard inverse-trig derivatives. A student who has not covered Unit 3 would not reliably know this antiderivative.

Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to evaluate the definite integral (Unit 6, topic 6.7: 'The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Definite Integrals'). The CED's EK CHA-4.A.1 states 'The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus states that if f is continuous on [a,b] and F is an antiderivative of f on [a,b], then ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a).' This is core AB/BC content.

Evaluating arctan(1) = π/4 and arctan(0) = 0 requires familiarity with standard inverse-trig values. While not explicitly a Unit 3 topic, these are standard values taught alongside inverse-trig derivatives (Unit 3, topic 3.4) and are prerequisite knowledge for any inverse-trig calculus work. Unit 2 covers basic trig values; inverse-trig values are a natural extension.

uncertainty_flags: Unit 2 vs. Unit 3 boundary: The antiderivative arctan(x) is most directly grounded in Unit 3 (inverse-trig derivatives). However, the CED's Unit 2 topic 2.7 lists 'Derivatives of cos x, sin x, e^x, and ln x' as core rules, and Unit 3 topic 3.4 extends this to inverse trig. A student who has completed Unit 3 will certainly know this; a student who has only completed Unit 2 may not. Marked Unit 3 as required, Unit 2 as supporting.

Distractor B (π/6) is mathematically coherent but its rationale ('This corresponds to arctan(1/√3)') is somewhat cryptic — it may not be immediately clear to a student why this is a plausible wrong answer without working through the error. This is acceptable for an MCQ distractor but worth noting.

No calculator required for this item despite BC exam context — the evaluation of arctan(1) = π/4 is a standard value, not a numerical approximation. Item is appropriately placed in a no-calculator section if used on a practice exam.

findings: MCQ structure complete: stem, four choices, one keyed answer (A), rationales for all four options present.
Keyed answer A is mathematically correct: arc length formula ∫√(1+(dy/dx)²)dx with y′=(3/2)x^(1/2), so (y′)²=(9/4)x, yielding ∫[0,1]√(1+(9/4)x)dx.

All four distractors are mathematically coherent near-miss errors: B omits squaring the derivative; C squares only the coefficient (3/2) instead of the full derivative; D squares the original function instead of its derivative.
Rationales are concise and accurate for all choices.

scope_violation.evidence: Arc length of a smooth planar curve is Topic 8.13, explicitly BC-only per the CED (tagged three times: title, Learning Objective CHA-6.A, EK CHA-6.A.1). This is a BC-eligible item. No AB scope violation.

criterion_units.evidence: Topic 8.13 (Arc Length of a Smooth Planar Curve, BC-only). The item requires the student to recognize and apply the arc-length formula ∫√(1+(dy/dx)²)dx, compute the derivative y′=(3/2)x^(1/2), square it to get (9/4)x, and substitute into the integrand. This is the core procedural content of Topic 8.13.

Distractor B represents a common procedural error: failing to square the derivative before adding it to 1 under the radical. This tests whether the student has internalized the structural requirement of the arc-length formula (the derivative must be squared). Appropriate near-miss for Topic 8.13.

Distractor C squares only the coefficient (3/2)→(9/4) but applies it to x instead of x^(1/2), yielding (9/4)x instead of (9/4)x. This tests whether the student correctly applies the chain rule / power rule to the full derivative (3/2)x^(1/2), not just its coefficient. Appropriate near-miss for Topic 8.13.

Distractor D squares the original function y=x^(3/2) instead of its derivative, yielding (x^(3/2))²=x³. This tests a fundamental conceptual error: confusing the arc-length formula's requirement to square the derivative with squaring the function itself. Appropriate near-miss for Topic 8.13.

uncertainty_flags: The item is a straightforward procedural MCQ testing arc-length formula application. No ambiguity in the mathematics or the scope assignment.

All distractors are mathematically sound and represent genuine, documented error patterns (derivative not squared, partial squaring, function vs. derivative confusion). No distractor is implausibly wrong.

The item does not require a graphing calculator or numerical approximation; it is a pure symbolic setup question, appropriate for the no-calculator MCQ section (Section I, Part A) if assigned there, or Part B if assigned there. No calculator-labeling issue.
No cross-unit dependencies: the item requires only Unit 8 content (arc length) and basic derivative rules (Unit 2). No Unit 9 or 10 content is involved.

findings: Item is a single-select MCQ with four choices and one keyed correct answer (B).
Stem is clear and unambiguous: evaluate dy/dx at a specific parameter value for a parametric curve.
All four choice rationales are present and substantive.
Correct answer (B) uses the parametric-derivative formula dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), evaluated at t=1: (3·1²−1)/(2·1) = 2/2 = 1. Verified correct.

Distractor A (0): rationale states 'numerator is not zero at 1' — correct; dy/dt = 3t²−1 = 3(1)−1 = 2 ≠ 0. Plausible misconception: student might confuse horizontal tangent (dy/dx=0, requiring dy/dt=0) with some other condition.
Distractor C (2): rationale 'uses only dx/dt' — at t=1, dx/dt = 2t = 2. Plausible misconception: student forgets the division and reports only the denominator.

Distractor D (3): rationale 'uses only part of dy/dt' — at t=1, dy/dt = 3t²−1 = 2, but if a student computed 3t² = 3 and forgot the −1, they'd get 3. Plausible misconception: incomplete differentiation of the y-component.
All distractors are mathematically coherent near-miss errors, not arbitrary wrong numbers.

scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses parametric-curve differentiation (dy/dx for parametric equations), which is Topic 9.1 (Defining and Differentiating Parametric Equations) in Unit 9. Unit 9 is BC-only and is within the BC exam scope. The CED's EK CHA-3.G.2 explicitly requires the formula dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), provided dx/dt ≠ 0. No exclusion applies. Item is in scope for BC.

criterion_units.evidence: The item requires the student to apply the parametric-derivative formula dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) at a specific parameter value. This is the core content of Topic 9.1, EK CHA-3.G.2. The CED states this formula explicitly: 'dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), provided dx/dt does not equal zero.' The item evaluates this formula at t=1, where dx/dt = 2 ≠ 0, so the condition is satisfied. A student who has not covered Unit 9 (parametric equations) cannot earn full credit on this item, as the parametric-derivative formula is not part of AB scope.

The item requires correct differentiation of the parametric components: dx/dt = d/dt(t²+1) = 2t and dy/dt = d/dt(t³−t) = 3t²−1. These are applications of the power rule (Unit 2, Topic 2.5) and the sum/difference rule (Unit 2, Topic 2.6). A student without Unit 2 coverage could not correctly compute these derivatives. However, Unit 2 is shared AB/BC and is prerequisite to Unit 9, so it is not a *required* unit for this item in the sense of the rubric definition — a student who has covered Unit 9 has necessarily covered Unit 2. The primary unit is Unit 9.

uncertainty_flags: The item does not explicitly state that t=1 is within the domain of the parametric curve or that dx/dt ≠ 0 at t=1. However, the CED's EK CHA-3.G.2 includes the proviso 'provided dx/dt does not equal zero,' and at t=1, dx/dt = 2 ≠ 0, so the condition is satisfied. No ambiguity in the mathematical setup.

Distractor D's rationale ('uses only part of dy/dt') is slightly informal — it could be clearer that the misconception is computing 3t² without the −1 term. However, the rationale is intelligible and the numeric value 3 is indeed what results from that error, so the distractor is sound.

The item is a straightforward procedural application of the parametric-derivative formula with no representation change, justification, or contextual reasoning. It aligns with Mathematical Practice 1 (Implementing Mathematical Processes) at the procedural level. This is appropriate for an MCQ but represents a lower-complexity item within the Unit 9 scope.

findings: All four choices are mathematically well-formed limit expressions.
Rationales for each distractor are concise and accurate.
Canonical answer D is correct: lim(h→0)[f′(2+h)−f′(2)]/h is the definition of f″(2).
No calculator required; notation is standard.

scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses the definition of the second derivative as the limit of the first derivative's difference quotient. This is core Unit 2 (Differentiation: Definition and Fundamental Properties, topic 2.2) and Unit 3 (topic 3.6, Higher-Order Derivatives) content, shared AB/BC. No BC-only content, no excluded topics, no out-of-scope methods.

criterion_units.evidence: Topic 3.6 (Calculating Higher-Order Derivatives) requires students to understand that f″(x) is the derivative of f′(x), and thus must be computed via the limit definition applied to f′. The item directly tests this conceptual foundation.

Topic 2.2 (Defining the Derivative of a Function and Using Derivative Notation) establishes that f′(a) = lim(h→0)[f(a+h)−f(a)]/h. The item applies this same structure to f′ in place of f, requiring fluency with the definition itself.

uncertainty_flags: Distractor B uses f′(2+h)−f′(h) with a fixed denominator 2, which is mathematically nonsensical as a second-derivative limit (the denominator should scale with h). The rationale 'Uses inconsistent base inputs and a fixed denominator' is accurate but could be more explicit: the denominator 2 is a constant, not a vanishing quantity, so the limit does not converge to a derivative. This is a strong distractor for students who confuse the structure of the difference quotient.

Distractor C uses lim(x→2) instead of lim(h→0), which shifts the conceptual error from 'wrong denominator' to 'wrong variable of approach.' The rationale 'Divides by the point rather than the change in input' correctly identifies this, but a student might still select C if they conflate the limit-definition form lim(x→a)[f(x)−f(a)]/(x−a) (which is equivalent to the h-form) with the second-derivative case. The item does not explicitly test whether students recognize these two forms as equivalent, so C remains a plausible distractor for that reason, though the fixed denominator 2 (not x−2) makes it clearly wrong.

findings: Item is a standard related-rates MCQ with four distractors tied to specific procedural errors.
Canonical answer D (7.2π cm³/s) is mathematically correct: V = (4/3)πr³ → dV/dt = 4πr²(dr/dt) = 4π(9)(0.2) = 7.2π.
All four distractors are grounded in documented misconceptions: surface-area formula (A), missing factor of 2 in chain rule (B), wrong volume coefficient (C).
No calculator required; stem correctly states 'No calculator is permitted.'
Distractor rationales are precise and pedagogically sound.

scope_violation.evidence: Related rates (topic 4.5) is shared AB/BC content. Chain rule (topic 3.1) and implicit differentiation w.r.t. time (topic 4.5) are both AB-eligible. No BC-only content required.

criterion_units.evidence: The chain rule (topic 3.1) is required to differentiate V = (4/3)πr³ with respect to t, recognizing that r depends on t: dV/dt = dV/dr · dr/dt = 4πr² · dr/dt. Distractor B ('3.6π') captures the documented misconception of 'forgetting to also differentiate the inner function' (CED Building Math Practices note for topic 3.1).

Topic 4.5 (Solving Related Rates Problems) requires: (1) identifying the relationship between variables (V and r), (2) differentiating implicitly w.r.t. time, (3) substituting known values (r=3, dr/dt=0.2) to find dV/dt. The correct answer 7.2π demonstrates full execution. Distractors A and C represent common errors in the volume formula itself (surface area vs. volume, wrong coefficient), which are topic 4.5 failure modes.

uncertainty_flags: Distractor A's rationale states 'Omits the factor of 4 from the surface-area coefficient: pi r^2 dr/dt = pi(3)^2(0.2) = 1.8pi instead of 4 pi r^2 dr/dt.' This phrasing is slightly ambiguous — it appears to conflate the surface-area formula (4πr²) with a volume-derivative coefficient. The intended error is likely 'uses dV/dt = πr²(dr/dt) [surface area formula] instead of dV/dt = 4πr²(dr/dt) [correct volume derivative].' Recommend clarifying the distractor rationale to avoid reader confusion about whether the error is a formula mix-up or a missing constant.

Distractor B's rationale 'Omits a factor of 2 from differentiating the cubic' is terse. The full error is likely: dV/dr = 4πr² is correct, but the student computes dV/dr = 2πr² (missing the 4), yielding dV/dt = 2π(9)(0.2) = 3.6π. Recommend expanding the rationale to show the incorrect derivative step explicitly.
No ambiguity in the stem or answer choices themselves; the item is sound as written.

findings: Item is a calculator-required MCQ with a numeric answer to three decimal places, consistent with CED guidance on calculator-answer rounding conventions.
Stem clearly identifies the task: find acceleration (derivative of velocity) at a specific point.
All four distractors are grounded in documented misconceptions or plausible procedural errors, not arbitrary wrong numbers.
Canonical answer C (0.591) is mathematically correct: a(t) = d/dt[t·sin(t²) - 0.4] = sin(t²) + t·cos(t²)·2t = sin(t²) + 2t²·cos(t²); a(1.3) = sin(1.69) + 2(1.69)cos(1.69) ≈ 0.591.

scope_violation.evidence: Item requires only product rule (Unit 2, topic 2.8) and chain rule (Unit 3, topic 3.1), both shared AB/BC content. No BC-only topics (Units 9-10, or Unit 6 topics 6.12-6.13, or Unit 8 topic 8.13) are required. Calculator use is appropriate for numeric evaluation.

criterion_units.evidence: Differentiating v(t) = t·sin(t²) - 0.4 requires the product rule on the t·sin(t²) term (topic 2.8). Distractor A omits the sin(t²) term entirely, a documented misconception from the Units 1-3 deep-tier fact pack: 'Failure to present this structure will cost students the point they might have earned, even with a correct numerical answer.'

The chain rule (topic 3.1) is required to differentiate sin(t²) as cos(t²)·2t. Distractor B treats sin(t²) as constant, a documented misconception from the Units 1-3 deep-tier fact pack: 'Misapplying the chain rule by forgetting to also differentiate the inner function... e.g. failing to recognize the chain rule applies to sin²x, tan(2x−1), or e^(x²).' Distractor D confuses v(t) itself with a(t), a fundamental conceptual error.

The item requires calculator-based numeric evaluation of a(1.3) = sin(1.69) + 2(1.69)²cos(1.69) and rounding to three decimal places, consistent with CED guidance: 'results rounded or truncated to three places after the decimal point.' All distractors are plausible numeric outputs from partial or incorrect differentiation, not arbitrary values.

uncertainty_flags: Distractor A's rationale ('Omits the product-rule term sin(t^2) and keeps only 2t^2 cos(t^2)') suggests the error is a failure to apply the product rule correctly, but the phrasing could be clearer: the student appears to have computed only the derivative of sin(t²) (which is 2t·cos(t²)) and then evaluated at t=1.3, rather than omitting sin(t²) from the product-rule expansion. The distractor is mathematically sound but the rationale's wording is slightly ambiguous.

Distractor B's rationale ('Differentiates only the factor t and treats sin(t^2) as constant') is clear and well-grounded in the documented chain-rule misconception, but the phrasing 'treats sin(t^2) as constant' could be misread as 'treats the entire product as constant.' The intent is clear from context, but precision could be improved.

The item does not explicitly test whether a student can distinguish between v(t) and a(t) in a conceptual sense—it tests only the procedural ability to differentiate and evaluate. Distractor D catches the error of using v(1.3) instead of a(1.3), but a student who makes this error might still be able to correctly differentiate v(t) in isolation. This is not a flaw in the item, but a note on what it does and does not assess.

findings: MCQ structure complete: stem, four choices with rationales, one keyed answer.
All four distractors are mathematically plausible near-misses or common errors.

scope_violation.evidence: Mean Value Theorem (Unit 5, topic 5.1) is shared AB/BC content. The function f(x)=e^x and interval [0,1] are both within standard scope. No BC-only content required.

criterion_units.evidence: Correct answer requires: (1) recognizing MVT applies (f continuous and differentiable on [0,1]); (2) computing average rate of change (f(1)−f(0))/(1−0) = (e−1)/1 = e−1; (3) setting f'(c) = e−1, i.e., e^c = e−1; (4) solving c = ln(e−1). All steps are Unit 5 topic 5.1 (Mean Value Theorem) content.

Distractor A (1/2) represents the common error of using the interval midpoint without solving the derivative equation. This is a documented misconception pattern: confusing the location of the extremum (which might be at a midpoint in some contexts) with the MVT's requirement to solve f'(c) = average rate of change. Appropriate for Unit 5.

Distractor B (e−1) reports the required derivative value (the average rate of change) instead of solving for its input c. This is a high-quality near-miss: the student correctly computes (e−1)/1 = e−1 but then reports that value as the answer instead of solving e^c = e−1. Appropriate for Unit 5.

Distractor D (ln 2) is a plausible but unrelated logarithm. It may appeal to students who recognize that a logarithm is needed but misapply it (e.g., ln(2) from a garbled midpoint or symmetry reasoning). Appropriate for Unit 5.

uncertainty_flags: No ambiguity in the stem or answer choices.
The keyed answer and all distractors are mathematically sound and well-motivated.
Item difficulty is appropriate for Unit 5 (MVT is a core topic, but solving e^c = e−1 requires logarithmic reasoning, making this a mid-to-high-difficulty MCQ).

findings: Item is a calculator-required MCQ with a numeric answer.
Stem clearly specifies rounding to nearest thousandth.
Four distractors provided with documented rationales.

scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Unit 6) combined with the chain rule (Unit 3), both core AB/BC content. The accumulation function G(x) = ∫₀^(x²) cos(t³)dt requires FTC Part 1 (topic 6.4) and chain rule (topic 3.1) to differentiate. No BC-only content required.

criterion_units.evidence: Correct answer requires: (1) applying FTC Part 1 to recognize G′(x) = cos((x²)³) = cos(x⁶), then (2) applying chain rule to differentiate x² as the upper limit, yielding G′(x) = cos(x⁶) · 2x. At x=1.2: G′(1.2) = cos((1.2)⁶) · 2(1.2) = cos(2.985984) · 2.4 ≈ (−0.9868) · 2.4 ≈ −2.368, rounds to −2.371. Both Unit 3 (chain rule) and Unit 6 (FTC) are required to earn full credit.

Rationale states 'omits or misuses the derivative of the upper limit.' This error reflects failure to apply the chain rule to the upper limit x². A student might compute cos((1.2)⁶) ≈ −0.9868 and stop, omitting the factor 2x = 2.4 from the chain rule. This is a Unit 3 (chain rule) error, but the distractor's framing emphasizes the FTC application (Unit 6) as the primary concept being tested.

Rationale states 'drops the negative sign from the cosine value and omits a factor.' This suggests the student correctly applies chain rule (2x factor) but makes two errors: (1) sign error on cos(x⁶) ≈ −0.9868 → 0.9868, and (2) possibly omits the 2x factor or applies it incorrectly. Requires both Unit 3 (chain rule mechanics) and Unit 6 (FTC sign handling) to refute.

Rationale states 'uses the correct magnitude but loses the negative sign.' This indicates the student correctly computes |G′(1.2)| ≈ 2.371 (correct application of both FTC and chain rule) but makes a sign error, likely mishandling the negative value of cos(x⁶) at x=1.2. Requires understanding of both Unit 3 (chain rule) and Unit 6 (FTC, including sign preservation) to refute.

uncertainty_flags: The item requires numerical evaluation of cos(2.985984) via graphing calculator. The exact numeric value depends on calculator precision and rounding convention. The stated answer −2.371 is consistent with standard rounding to three decimal places, but verification requires independent calculator execution.

Distractor B's rationale ('omits or misuses the derivative of the upper limit') is somewhat ambiguous — it could mean the student applies FTC without the chain rule, or applies chain rule incorrectly. The distinction affects whether this is purely a Unit 3 error or a combined Unit 3/6 error. Treated as Unit 6 primary per the rationale's emphasis on 'upper limit' (FTC concept).

Distractor C's rationale ('omits a factor') is vague — it is unclear whether the omitted factor is the 2x from the chain rule, or a factor from the cosine evaluation. Treated as requiring both Unit 3 and Unit 6 per the compound nature of the error.

findings: Item is a single-select MCQ with four choices and one keyed correct answer (C).
Stem is self-contained and unambiguous: find area between two curves on a closed interval.
All four distractors are justified with plausible error modes (single-boundary integration, endpoint-value subtraction, addition instead of subtraction).
No calculator permitted, consistent with Section I Part A scope.
Correct answer (1/6) is mathematically sound: ∫₀¹(√x − x)dx = [⅔x^(3/2) − ½x²]₀¹ = ⅔ − ½ = 1/6.

scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses finding area between two curves expressed as functions of x on a closed interval. This is Topic 8.4 (Unit 8, AB/BC shared content). No BC-only techniques (parametric arc length, polar area, series, improper integrals) are required. Item is eligible for both AB and BC exams.

criterion_units.evidence: Correct answer requires: (1) identifying which curve is the upper boundary (√x > x on [0,1]); (2) setting up the definite integral ∫₀¹(√x − x)dx; (3) antidifferentiating both terms (⅔x^(3/2) for √x, −½x² for −x); (4) evaluating at endpoints and subtracting. All steps are Topic 8.4 (Area Between Curves as Functions of x) and Topic 6.7/6.8 (antidifferentiation via power rule, a Unit 6 prerequisite).

Rationale states 'Integrates only one boundary correctly.' This error mode (computing ∫₀¹√x dx = ⅔ alone, omitting the subtraction of ∫₀¹x dx = ½) tests whether the student recognizes that area *between* curves requires a difference of two integrals, not a single integral. Assesses Topic 8.4's core requirement: setting up the correct integrand as (top − bottom).

Rationale states 'Subtracts endpoint values rather than areas.' This error (computing √1 − 1 − (√0 − 0) = 0, or a variant endpoint-value subtraction) tests a documented misconception: confusing the Fundamental Theorem's evaluation step [F(b) − F(a)] with a direct subtraction of function values. Assesses Topic 8.4's requirement to integrate, not merely evaluate endpoints.

Rationale states 'Adds rather than subtracts the two component integrals.' This error (computing ∫₀¹√x dx + ∫₀¹x dx = ⅔ + ½ = 7/6, or a variant addition) tests whether the student recognizes the sign in the area-between-curves integrand. Assesses Topic 8.4's core requirement: the integrand must be (top − bottom), not (top + bottom).

uncertainty_flags: No uncertainty. Item is straightforward Topic 8.4 (Area Between Curves, Functions of x) with no BC-only content, no ambiguous stem, and all four distractors grounded in documented error modes (single-boundary omission, endpoint-value confusion, sign error). Keyed answer is mathematically correct and all distractors are plausible near-misses.

findings: MCQ stem is clear and self-contained.
Four distinct numeric distractors provided, each with documented error rationale.
Calculator requirement stated and appropriate for numeric integration.
All answer choices are distinct and plausible.

scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses volume with cross sections (Unit 8, topics 8.7-8.8), a shared AB/BC topic. No BC-only content (arc length, parametric/polar/vector functions, series) is required. Item is AB-eligible.

criterion_units.evidence: Item requires identifying that cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are semicircles with diameter e^(−x²), then computing the area of a semicircle as (1/2)π(d/2)² = πd²/8. This is the core Unit 8.7-8.8 skill: setting up the correct cross-sectional area formula.

Item requires computing ∫₀^1.5 (π/8)[e^(−x²)]² dx = (π/8)∫₀^1.5 e^(−2x²) dx numerically. This is Unit 6 (definite integral evaluation) applied in the Unit 8 context; calculator is required and appropriate per the stimulus.

Item asks for the answer 'to the nearest thousandth,' requiring proper rounding of a calculator result. Per the 2025/2026 Scoring Guidelines' universal front-matter note on calculator answers, rounding to three decimal places is the standard convention.

uncertainty_flags: Distractor B (0.491) uses π/4 instead of π/8. This is a plausible error (using the full semicircle-area coefficient π/4 instead of the correct π/8), but the rationale should clarify whether this represents forgetting to divide by 2 (semicircle vs. full circle) or a different conceptual slip. As written, it is clear enough.

Distractor D (1.963) treats the diameter as the radius and uses a full circle. This is a compound error (two mistakes: diameter→radius confusion, and semicircle→full-circle confusion). The rationale is accurate but the error is somewhat artificial. However, it is a plausible distractor for a student who misreads the problem.
The stem does not explicitly state that the solid extends from z=0 upward, but this is standard convention for 'base' problems and is clear from context. No ambiguity flag needed.
No uncertainty regarding unit scope or calculator appropriateness.

findings: Item is a single-select MCQ with four distractors and one keyed correct answer (B).
Stem is clear and unambiguous: asks for speed (magnitude of velocity vector) at a specific time, to three decimal places.
Calculator requirement is stated and appropriate: numeric evaluation of transcendental functions and square roots is required.
All four distractors are refutable against the keyed answer and represent plausible misconceptions (component-only errors, addition vs. Euclidean norm).

scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses vector-valued function differentiation and speed calculation (Unit 9, Topics 9.4-9.6). All content is within BC scope. No AB-only or excluded content is required.

criterion_units.evidence: Correct answer requires: (1) differentiating the vector-valued function r(t) = ⟨t² − 2t, e^(−t)⟩ to obtain r'(t) = ⟨2t − 2, −e^(−t)⟩ (Topic 9.4, EK CHA-3.H.1: 'Methods for calculating derivatives of real-valued functions can be extended to vector-valued functions'); (2) evaluating at t = 1.4 to get r'(1.4) = ⟨0.8, −e^(−1.4)⟩ ≈ ⟨0.8, −0.2466⟩; (3) computing speed as the magnitude ||r'(1.4)|| = √(0.8² + (−e^(−1.4))²) ≈ √(0.64 + 0.0608) ≈ √0.7008 ≈ 0.837 (Topic 9.6, FUN-8.B.1: speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector). The CED does not supply an explicit componentwise formula for vector-valued derivatives in its required-content text (see Units 9-10 deep-tier detail, Topics 9.4-9.6), but the extension principle is explicit and the speed-as-magnitude concept is stated verbatim in FUN-8.B.1.

Distractor A (0.247) represents the magnitude of only the vertical (y-component) velocity: |dy/dt| = |−e^(−1.4)| ≈ 0.247. This is a component-only error, not the Euclidean norm. Refuted by the definition of speed in Topic 9.6 (FUN-8.B.1), which requires the magnitude of the entire velocity vector, not a single component.

Distractor C (0.800) represents the magnitude of only the horizontal (x-component) velocity: |dx/dt| = |2(1.4) − 2| = |0.8| = 0.8. This is a component-only error. Refuted by the same definition of speed (Topic 9.6, FUN-8.B.1).

Distractor D (1.047) represents the sum of component magnitudes: |dx/dt| + |dy/dt| ≈ 0.8 + 0.247 ≈ 1.047. This is a common misconception: adding magnitudes instead of using the Euclidean norm √(a² + b²). Refuted by the definition of speed as the magnitude of the velocity vector (Topic 9.6, FUN-8.B.1), which requires the square-root-of-sum-of-squares formula, not a linear sum.

findings: MCQ structure well-formed: one correct answer (B), three distractors with documented rationales.
Stem is clear and unambiguous.

scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses polar-curve area (Unit 9, Topic 9.8), which is BC-only and within scope. No AB content is required. The polar-area formula ∫(1/2)[r(θ)]² dθ is CED-adjacent (stated conceptually in EK CHA-5.D.1/D.2 as 'can be extended to polar coordinates'; the explicit formula is not in the CED text but is confirmed by real 2025 BC FRQ scoring data). The rose-curve r=2sin(3θ) is a standard illustrative example for polar-area problems and does not violate any exclusion.

criterion_units.evidence: Topic 9.8 (Area of a Polar Region or the Area Bounded by a Single Polar Curve). The item requires students to (1) identify the angular bounds of one petal of r=2sin(3θ), (2) apply the polar-area formula (1/2)∫[r(θ)]² dθ, and (3) evaluate the definite integral. Per the 2025 BC Scoring Guidelines and Chief Reader Report (BC2 Part B), the polar-area setup splits into three independent points: presence of squared-radius term, full correct integrand, and constant/limits/final value. This MCQ collapses those into a single numeric answer, but the underlying skill is Topic 9.8's core content. The rose curve r=2sin(3θ) has 3 petals (period 2π/3), each spanning an angular width of π/3. One petal corresponds to 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/3. The correct computation is (1/2)∫₀^(π/3) [2sin(3θ)]² dθ = (1/2)∫₀^(π/3) 4sin²(3θ) dθ = 2∫₀^(π/3) sin²(3θ) dθ. Using sin²(u) = (1−cos(2u))/2: = 2∫₀^(π/3) (1−cos(6θ))/2 dθ = ∫₀^(π/3) (1−cos(6θ)) dθ = [θ − sin(6θ)/6]₀^(π/3) = π/3 − sin(2π)/6 − 0 = π/3. Answer B is correct.

Identifying the angular interval for one petal of a rose curve r=a·sin(nθ) or r=a·cos(nθ) is a prerequisite skill for Topic 9.8 area computation. For r=2sin(3θ), the curve traces one complete petal when sin(3θ) goes from 0 to 1 and back to 0, i.e., 0 ≤ 3θ ≤ π, or 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/3. Distractor A (π/6) represents half this angular width, suggesting a student error in identifying the petal's full angular span. This error mode is documented in the distractor rationale and is plausible.

Once the angular bounds and formula are set, the student must evaluate (1/2)∫₀^(π/3) 4sin²(3θ) dθ. This requires knowledge of the double-angle identity sin²(u) = (1−cos(2u))/2 and antidifferentiation of constant and cosine terms. The correct result is π/3. Distractors C (2π/3, doubling the result) and D (π, an unrelated scale) represent plausible computational errors or conceptual confusions about the final scaling.

uncertainty_flags: The polar-area formula (1/2)∫[r(θ)]² dθ is not explicitly written in the CED's required-content text for Topic 9.8 (EK CHA-5.D.1/D.2 state only that rectangular area concepts 'can be extended to polar coordinates'). However, this formula is confirmed by real 2025 BC FRQ scoring data (BC2 Part B) and is universally taught and tested. The item is well-grounded in real exam practice, not merely in CED text.

The rose-curve family r=a·sin(nθ) and r=a·cos(nθ) is a standard illustrative example in AP Calculus BC pedagogy but is not explicitly named in the CED's required content. The item assumes students have encountered this family in instruction. This is a low-risk assumption given the prevalence of rose curves in released BC FRQs and practice materials, but it is not a CED-mandated example.

No calculator is required or permitted for this item. The symbolic computation (double-angle identity, antidifferentiation, evaluation) is entirely algebraic. This aligns with the MCQ Section I, Part A (no calculator, 62 minutes) structure, though the item could also appear in Part B (calculator permitted) without requiring calculator use.

findings: MCQ structure well-formed: one correct answer (C), three distractors with distinct rationales.

Topic 1.8 (Squeeze Theorem) is a limit-evaluation tool for bounding a function between two others as x approaches a point, not a tool for guaranteeing function values on an interval. Rationale correctly identifies Squeeze Theorem's purpose.

findings: MCQ stem is clear and unambiguous.

criterion_units.evidence: Topic 2.7 (Derivatives of e^x) establishes that d/dx[e^x] = e^x. Topic 3.1 (The Chain Rule) requires students to recognize that d/dx[e^u] = e^u·u' when u is a composite function. The item directly tests this combination: u = 5x², u' = 10x, so d/dx[e^(5x²)] = e^(5x²)·10x. The fact pack's Units 1-3 deep-tier detail explicitly documents this as a high-error pattern: 'Documented misconception (chain rule on exponentials, boundary with Unit 3 but rooted in Unit 2 derivative rules): per the Chief Reader Report, students frequently differentiate e^u as u·e^u instead of e^u·u′ — i.e. they apply a garbled product-rule-shaped pattern to what should be a direct chain-rule application of a known derivative rule.' Distractor C (5x²·e^(5x²)) directly instantiates this documented misconception.

uncertainty_flags: Distractor D (e^(10x)) is mathematically incoherent as a plausible near-miss; it appears to conflate the exponent derivative (10x) with the base, which is a weaker misconception signal than A, B, or C. It remains a valid distractor but is less grounded in documented student error than the others.
The item is calculator-not-required (purely symbolic differentiation), consistent with Section I Part A (no-calculator MCQ). No calculator capability is invoked or needed.

findings: Item is a single-select MCQ with four choices and one keyed correct answer (B).

Rationale for choice D cites a real error: confusing f(1) (function value) with f'(1) (derivative value).

scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses the chain rule (Unit 3, Topic 3.1) applied to a composite function h(x)=f(x²) where the outer function is given via a table of derivatives. Evaluation at x=1 requires substituting x=1 into both the chain-rule formula and the table lookup for f'(1).

The item requires reading f'(1)=6 from the table and correctly distinguishing it from f(1)=4 (choice D distractor) and from f'(2)=-3 (choice C distractor). This tests Practice 2 (Connecting Representations) — translating from tabular representation to symbolic chain-rule computation.

findings: Stem is clear and self-contained.
All four distractors are mathematically coherent and represent documented or plausible error patterns.
Canonical answer A is correct: g(1) = 1³ + 1 = 2, so g⁻¹(2) = 1; g'(x) = 3x² + 1, so g'(1) = 4; (g⁻¹)'(2) = 1/g'(1) = 1/4.
Distractor B (choice 4) represents failure to apply the reciprocal in the inverse-derivative formula — a real, documented misconception.
Distractor C (choice 1/13) represents evaluating g' at the wrong input (x=2 instead of x=1), yielding g'(2) = 3(4) + 1 = 13, then taking reciprocal — a plausible near-miss.
Distractor D (choice 1) confuses the inverse function's value with its derivative — a real conceptual error.
No calculator required; purely symbolic work.

scope_violation.evidence: Item assesses the inverse-function derivative formula (Topic 3.3, EK FUN-3.B.4: 'The derivative of an inverse function can be found using the relationship (f⁻¹)'(x) = 1/f'(f⁻¹(x))'), which is shared AB/BC content. No BC-only topics (Units 9–10, Topics 6.12–6.13) are required. The cubic polynomial g(x) = x³ + x is elementary and requires only Unit 2 derivative rules (power rule, sum rule). The item is AB-eligible and appropriately tagged as BC.

criterion_units.evidence: The keyed solution requires finding g⁻¹(2) by solving g(x) = 2, i.e., x³ + x = 2. This is implicit in the inverse-function-derivative formula (Topic 3.3, EK FUN-3.B.4) and is a prerequisite step that all correct and most near-miss responses must execute. Distractor C's error (evaluating g' at x=2 instead of x=1) hinges on failing this step.

The keyed solution requires computing g'(x) = 3x² + 1 (Unit 2, power rule and sum rule, Topics 2.5–2.6) and evaluating it at x=1 to get g'(1) = 4. Distractor B represents computing g'(1) correctly but failing to apply the reciprocal, confirming that the derivative computation itself is a separable skill.

The keyed solution applies the inverse-function-derivative formula (g⁻¹)'(2) = 1/g'(g⁻¹(2)) = 1/g'(1) = 1/4 (Topic 3.3, EK FUN-3.B.4). Distractor B (choice 4) represents omitting the reciprocal step entirely — a direct test of whether the formula is known and applied. Distractor D (choice 1) represents confusing the inverse function's value with its derivative, a conceptual error at the formula level.

uncertainty_flags: Distractor C's error (evaluating g' at x=2 instead of x=1) is plausible but not explicitly documented in the fact pack's Chief Reader Report or Scoring Guidelines. It represents a coherent near-miss (correct formula structure, wrong input to g') but is not confirmed as a real, high-frequency student error. The rationale is sound, but the distractor's prevalence is not independently verified.

The item does not require a calculator and is purely symbolic, consistent with MCQ Part A (no-calculator) scope. findings: Item stem is clear and unambiguous.

scope_violation.evidence: Implicit differentiation of a polynomial equation is core Unit 3 content (topic 3.2), assessed on both AB and BC exams. No BC-only content required. No calculator capability required or implied.

criterion_units.evidence: Topic 3.2 (Implicit Differentiation). The CED's own Building Math Practices note flags 'using dy where dy/dx is meant' as a documented misconception. The 2025 Chief Reader Report confirms this is a real, reader-documented error pattern: 'Using dy where dy/dx is meant, or dy/dx where the operator d/dx is meant (conflating the differential with the derivative).' Choice B correctly applies the chain rule to y^3 (yielding 3y^2 · dy/dx) and differentiates x^2 as 2x, then sets the result equal to 0 (the derivative of the constant 10). This matches the required structure for implicit differentiation.

Choice A (2x + 3y^2 dy = 0) uses the differential 'dy' where the derivative notation 'dy/dx' is required. This is a documented notation error from the Chief Reader Report's explicit list of implicit-differentiation misconceptions. The fact pack notes: 'Using dy where dy/dx is meant... conflating the differential with the derivative.' This is a strong, real, quotable distractor grounded in actual student error.

Choice C (2x + 3y^2/dx = 0) uses nonsensical mixed notation, dividing by dx alone rather than expressing the derivative as dy/dx. This is a plausible near-miss for a student who recognizes that dx belongs in the denominator but fails to construct the proper dy/dx ratio. Appropriate as a notation-confusion distractor.

Choice D (2 + 3y^2 (dy/dx) = 0) uses correct notation but contains a differentiation error: the derivative of x^2 is 2x, not 2. This is a procedural slip (dropping the x), not a notation issue. Appropriate as a distractor for students who understand notation but make an arithmetic or rule-application error on the power rule.

uncertainty_flags: The item tests notation precision (dy vs. dy/dx) rather than the full implicit-differentiation process. While notation is explicitly scored in AP Calc (per the fact pack's Unit 3 deep-tier detail), this item does not assess whether the student can complete a full implicit-differentiation problem or solve for dy/dx. It is a narrow, notation-focused MCQ, which is appropriate for Part A (no calculator, 62 minutes, 29 questions) but represents only one facet of Unit 3 competency.

The equation x^2 + y^3 = 10 is simple enough that all distractors are clearly distinguishable. A more complex equation (e.g., involving products or quotients requiring the product/quotient rule) would test whether students can apply the chain rule correctly while maintaining notation precision, but this item does not require that depth.

scope_violation.evidence: The question assesses precipitation stoichiometry (Unit 4.5, 4.7), net ionic equations (Unit 4.2), and gravimetric analysis with systematic error identification (Unit 4.6 titration context + laboratory reasoning). All content is within the assessed scope. The stimulus (AgNO₃ + excess chloride) is a standard precipitation scenario. No phase diagrams, colligative properties, Arrhenius calculations, or other excluded topics are invoked.

criterion_units.evidence: Part (a) requires molar-mass bridging (Unit 1.1: n = m/M applied in reverse via molarity M = n/V) and stoichiometric calculation from balanced equation (Unit 4.5). The net ionic equation itself is Unit 4.2. A student who has not covered Unit 1 molar-mass concepts cannot reliably convert molarity and volume to moles; a student who has not covered Unit 4 stoichiometry and net ionic equations cannot write or interpret the equation.

Part (b) requires understanding stoichiometric ratios from balanced equations (Unit 4.5) and the concept of limiting reagent / completion assumption (Unit 4.5). The 1:1 mole ratio is read directly from the net ionic equation coefficients. A student who has not covered Unit 4 stoichiometry cannot justify why moles of AgCl equal moles of Ag+.

Part (c) describes a gravimetric procedure (Unit 4.6 introduction to titration / quantitative analysis context) and requires conversion of measured mass back to moles (Unit 1.1: n = m/M). Drying to constant mass, cooling in a desiccator, and controlled washing are standard laboratory techniques for minimizing systematic error. A student who has not covered Unit 1 molar mass cannot convert the measured AgCl mass to moles; a student who has not covered Unit 4 quantitative analysis cannot design or describe a gravimetric verification procedure.

Part (d) requires identifying a systematic error in a gravimetric procedure and predicting its directional effect on the calculated result (Unit 4.6 and Science Practice 2: experimental design and error analysis). The connection between incomplete drying (higher measured mass → higher calculated moles) and precipitate loss (lower measured mass → lower calculated moles) is a direct application of error propagation in stoichiometric calculations. A student who has not covered Unit 4 quantitative analysis and experimental reasoning cannot reliably predict error direction.

uncertainty_flags: Part (b) uses the phrase 'precipitation went to completion' — the canonical answer clarifies this means 'essentially all Ag+ is consumed' (the limiting reagent), not that the reaction reaches 100% conversion in a thermodynamic sense. The rubric criterion 'states the completion assumption' should be interpreted as 'states that Ag+ is the limiting reagent and is essentially fully consumed because Cl- is in excess,' not as a claim about absolute equilibrium. This is consistent with Unit 4.5 stoichiometry language but could be clearer in the stem.

Part (c) asks students to 'describe a gravimetric procedure' but does not specify whether they must name the apparatus (filter paper, Büchner funnel, desiccator) or whether a functional description suffices. The canonical answer names desiccator but the rubric criterion says 'Credit filtration/collection, washing, drying to constant mass and cooling before weighing' — apparatus naming is not explicitly required. This is acceptable (procedural understanding is the goal), but item authors should confirm the rubric aligns with their grading intent.

Part (d) asks for 'one systematic error' and the canonical answer provides two examples (incomplete drying and precipitate loss). The rubric criterion says 'Accepts incomplete drying as high, or transfer/filtration loss as low' — this correctly allows either error, but the stem's singular 'one' could be misread as requiring exactly one. The rubric is correct; the stem is slightly ambiguous but not incorrect.

The stimulus states 'excess chloride' without specifying the source (e.g., NaCl solution, HCl, or another chloride salt). This is intentional (the source does not affect the stoichiometry), but a student might ask whether the excess chloride's identity matters for the net ionic equation. The canonical answer correctly shows Ag+ + Cl- → AgCl(s), which is independent of the chloride source. This is not a scope violation but a minor pedagogical note.

findings: Criterion b2 awards 2 points for solving the Ka expression and obtaining [H3O+], but the rubric does not explicitly require showing the quadratic solution or small-x approximation validation. Per CED 8.3 and 2025 SG patterns, the approximation check (x/0.150 < 5%) should be a separate, explicit criterion point, not bundled into b2.

Criterion e1 asks students to justify the small-x approximation validity, but part (e) of the stem explicitly asks this question. The rubric should clarify whether part (e) is scored separately (1 point) or whether the approximation justification in b2 satisfies both b2 and e1 — currently ambiguous.

Criterion c1 states 'from the student's own [H3O+]' but does not specify significant-figure requirements. The canonical answer gives pH ≈ 2.85 (2 decimal places) from [H3O+] ≈ 1.4 × 10^−3 M (2 sig figs), which is correct, but the rubric should make this explicit.

criterion_units.evidence: Topic 8.3 (Weak Acid and Base Equilibria): EK requires writing Ka expressions for weak acids. The criterion asks for the equilibrium expression C2H5COOH(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + C2H5COO−(aq) and Ka = [H3O+][C2H5COO−]/[C2H5COOH]. This is a direct application of 8.3.A.1.

Topic 8.3 (Weak Acid and Base Equilibria): EK requires setting up ICE tables to track concentration changes. The criterion asks for initial [C2H5COOH] = 0.150 M, products = 0, and change row −x, +x, +x. This is foundational to 8.3.A.2.

Topic 8.3 (Weak Acid and Base Equilibria): EK requires solving Ka expressions to find equilibrium [H3O+]. The criterion asks for solving Ka = x²/(0.150 − x) ≈ x²/0.150 = 1.3 × 10^−5, yielding x ≈ 1.4 × 10^−3 M. This is 8.3.A.2. The small-x approximation validity check (x/0.150 < 5%) is part of the same calculation but is separately assessed in criterion e1.
Topic 8.1 (Introduction to Acids and Bases): EK requires calculating pH from [H3O+] using pH = −log[H3O+]. The criterion asks for pH ≈ −log(1.4 × 10^−3) ≈ 2.85. This is 8.1.A.1.

Topic 7.9–7.10 (Le Châtelier's Principle): EK requires predicting system response to dilution. Topic 8.3 (Weak Acid Equilibria): EK requires understanding percent dissociation. The criterion asks students to predict that percent dissociation *increases* upon dilution (even though [H3O+] decreases in absolute terms) and justify via Le Châtelier's principle — dilution shifts equilibrium toward the side with more dissolved particles. This bridges 7.10 (Q ≠ K after disturbance) and 8.3 (percent ionization definition).

Topic 8.3 (Weak Acid and Base Equilibria): EK requires understanding when the small-x approximation is valid. The criterion asks for justification that because Ka is small, x is small relative to 0.150 M, and the approximation is valid when x/[initial] < ~5%. This is a quantitative reasoning requirement within 8.3.A.2.

Topic 8.3 (Weak Acid and Base Equilibria): EK requires calculating percent ionization (percent dissociation). The criterion asks for percent dissociation = ([H3O+]/0.150) × 100% ≈ 0.93%. This is 8.3.A.2.

Topic 8.2 (pH and pOH of Strong Acids and Bases) vs. Topic 8.3 (Weak Acid and Base Equilibria): EK requires comparing strong-acid and weak-acid pH at the same initial concentration. The criterion asks students to state that 0.150 M HCl (strong acid, fully dissociates, [H3O+] = 0.150 M, pH ≈ 0.82) has lower pH than 0.150 M propanoic acid (weak acid, partially dissociates, [H3O+] ≈ 1.4 × 10^−3 M, pH ≈ 2.85) and explain via full vs. partial dissociation. This requires 8.2.A.1 (strong-acid pH) and 8.3.A.2 (weak-acid pH) in comparison.

Topic 6.3 (Heat Transfer and Thermal Equilibrium): EK states 'collisions transfer energy (heat transfer)' and 'warmer-body particles have greater average KE.' Justification requires connecting macroscopic temperature observation to microscopic heat-flow reasoning, which is 6.3 scope.

Topic 6.3 (Heat Transfer and Thermal Equilibrium): EK explicitly covers the bidirectional energy-transfer model — 'warmer-body particles have greater average KE; collisions transfer energy.' The criterion tests whether students distinguish 'system absorbs heat' from 'surroundings produce cold,' a direct 6.3 misconception target.

Topic 9.3 (Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability): EK requires understanding ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° and the sign-table shortcut for ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 (favored at high T). uncertainty_flags: Part (c) does not explicitly require students to state 'at room temperature' or 'at 25°C,' though the canonical answer includes this qualifier. The rubric criterion as written ('TΔS > ΔH') is temperature-independent in phrasing. A student who states 'TΔS outweighs ΔH' without specifying temperature should likely earn credit, but the rubric could be more explicit about whether temperature-context is required or merely helpful. Recommend clarifying: 'at room temperature, the TΔS term is large enough that...' to match the canonical answer's precision.

The criterion for part (b) uses the phrase 'correctly using energy or heat language' — this is appropriately targeted at the documented misconception (2025 CRR: students often say 'the system produces cold' rather than 'the surroundings lose heat'), but the rubric does not explicitly list example wrong phrasings that would *not* earn credit. A student who says 'the dissolution makes the water cold' (passive voice, ambiguous agency) might be borderline. Recommend adding a distractor example to the rubric for scorer consistency.

Part (a) splits identification from justification into two separate 1-point criteria. The criterion text ('To earn this point, explicitly show...') suggests part-a and part-a-2 are independent, which is correct, but a brief note ('Each part is scored independently') would remove ambiguity.

The canonical answer for part (c) uses the phrase 'ordered solid lattice separates into dispersed, mobile, solvated ions' — this is precise and excellent. The rubric criterion simplifies to 'ordered solid separates into dispersed, solvated ions.' A student who says 'the solid breaks apart into ions in solution' (omitting 'dispersed' or 'solvated') should likely earn credit for the core ΔS > 0 reasoning, but the rubric does not clarify the minimum specificity required. Recommend: 'ΔS is positive because the solid's ordered structure becomes a dispersed solution of ions' as the minimum acceptable phrasing.

findings: Criterion a1 (2 points) requires both Ksp setup AND numerical solution. The rubric does not specify acceptable error tolerance (e.g., ±0.1 × 10^-4 M) or significant-figure expectations. Per the fact pack's General Conventions, a 3-sig-fig concentration (1.1 × 10^-4 M) should yield a pOH/pH to 3 decimal places if derived; the rubric should clarify whether intermediate rounding is penalized.

Criterion a2 (1 point) requires Le Chatelier reasoning but does not explicitly require the student to identify H+ + OH- → H2O as the mechanism by which [OH-] decreases. The rubric text 'reacts with and lowers [OH-]' is vague about whether a bare statement suffices or whether the neutralization reaction must be shown.

Criterion a3 (1 point) conflates two distinct concepts: 'common-ion effect' (the phenomenon) and 'Le Chatelier's principle' (the mechanism). The rubric should clarify whether naming the effect alone earns credit or whether mechanistic reasoning (Q > Ksp → precipitate forms, or equilibrium shifts left) is required. Per the fact pack's documented misconception from 2025 Q1 Part F, 'just memorizing that [a rule] did not help the student earn this point' — items should test mechanism, not memorized labels.

The rubric does not address error-carried-forward credit. If a student miscalculates s in a1 but then correctly applies that wrong value to a2 or a3, the fact pack's General Conventions note that 2025 SG 'repeatedly award[s] a later point consistent with an earlier (possibly wrong) part's answer.' This rubric does not specify whether a2/a3 reasoning is independent of a1's numerical result.

Criterion a1 does not specify whether units (M) are required. Per the fact pack's General Conventions, 'some rubric points explicitly do not require units or a sign to earn credit, while others explicitly do — this is stated point-by-point in the 2025 SG, not by a blanket exam-wide rule.' This rubric should state the requirement explicitly.

The stimulus provides Ksp = 5.61 × 10^-12 (3 sig figs). The canonical answer reports s ≈ 1.1 × 10^-4 M (2 sig figs). This rubric should clarify the acceptable sig-fig range.

criterion_units.evidence: Criterion a1 directly assesses Topic 7.11 (Introduction to Solubility Equilibria): 'solubility can be calculated from Ksp and vice versa (from molar solubility of a saturated solution).' The setup Ksp = [Mg2+][OH-]^2 = (s)(2s)^2 = 4s^3 and solution for s is the core EK of 7.11.

Criterion a2 assesses Topic 8.11 (pH and Solubility): 'a salt's solubility is pH-sensitive when a constituent ion is a weak acid, weak base, or hydroxide ion — understood qualitatively via Le Chatelier's principle.' The reasoning that lowering pH (increasing [H+]) consumes OH- and shifts the dissolution equilibrium rightward is the core EK of 8.11. This is also consistent with Topic 7.9 (Le Chatelier's Principle), but the pH-solubility link is explicitly Topic 8.11.

Criterion a3 assesses Topic 7.12 (Common-Ion Effect): 'a salt's solubility is reduced when dissolved into a solution already containing one of its constituent ions (common-ion effect) — understood qualitatively via Le Chatelier's principle or calculated from Ksp.' The reasoning that added Mg2+ (from Mg(NO3)2) shifts the Mg(OH)2 dissolution equilibrium leftward is the core EK of 7.12.

scope_violation.evidence: Stimulus and stem are entirely within Unit 1 (Kinematics, topics 1.2–1.3). criterion_units.evidence: Part (a) requires direct application of constant-acceleration kinematics equations v=v₀+at and Δx=v₀t+½at² (Unit 1, topic 1.3). A student who has not covered Unit 1 cannot earn full credit on this criterion because the equations themselves are Unit 1 content.

Part (b) requires two distinct competencies: (1) naming and justifying the constant-acceleration kinematics equations (Unit 1, topic 1.3), and (2) explaining that constant acceleration requires a constant net force via Newton's second law F_net=ma (Unit 2, topic 2.5). A student who has not covered Unit 2 cannot fully justify why the kinematics equations apply in this scenario, because the physical justification rests on Newton's second law. Both units are required for full credit.

uncertainty_flags: Part (b) asks for 'justification' of the kinematics equations via Newton's second law. The rubric criterion requires 'explicitly connects constant acceleration to a constant net force via F_net=ma.' findings: Part (a) criterion requires students to write Newton's second law for equilibrium (ΣF=0) and label all three forces with directions. The canonical answer correctly shows two valid configurations (anchor below: F_buoyant - mg - T = 0; anchor above: F_buoyant - mg + T = 0), but the rubric criterion specifies 'tension acting downward' as the only acceptable direction. This precludes full credit for a student who correctly derives the upward-anchor case in part (a) and then correctly eliminates it in part (b)—a valid two-part logical flow that the rubric blocks.

Part (a) criterion awards only 1 point for writing ΣF=0 with all three forces correctly identified and directed. However, the canonical answer shows that the direction of tension depends on the anchor location, which is not determined until part (b). The rubric should either (1) award part (a) credit for ΣF=0 with tension direction left open/justified by the density comparison, or (2) explicitly defer the tension-direction requirement to part (b) after the anchor location is established.

Part (b) criterion requires the conclusion 'anchor must be below' and the formula T=(ρ_water−ρ_block)gV. However, the rubric does not clarify whether a student who correctly reasons through part (a) with an upward-anchor configuration, then correctly eliminates it in part (b) via the density comparison, can earn full credit on part (b) even if their part (a) tension direction was opposite. The rubric should address follow-through/error-carried-forward credit explicitly.

The rubric does not specify whether the formula T=(ρ_water−ρ_block)gV must be derived algebraically from ΣF=0, or whether stating it with the density reasoning is sufficient. The canonical answer shows derivation; the criterion text does not require it.

criterion_units.evidence: Part (a) requires drawing a free-body diagram (Unit 2, topic 2.2 convention: forces as vectors originating from the object's center of mass, each labeled with direction) and writing Newton's second law for equilibrium ΣF=0 (Unit 2, topic 2.4). The three forces are: buoyant force F_b=ρ_water*g*V (Unit 8, topic 8.3, Archimedes' principle), weight mg=ρ_block*g*V (Unit 2, topic 2.6), and string tension (Unit 2, topic 2.3, Newton's third law / internal forces). The equilibrium condition ΣF=0 is Unit 2 (topic 2.4). However, the *identification* of the buoyant force and its magnitude formula is Unit 8-specific; without Unit 8, a student cannot earn full credit on this part.

Part (b) requires applying Archimedes' principle (Unit 8, topic 8.3: 'magnitude equals the weight of fluid displaced by the object, F_b=ρVg') to compare ρ_block vs. ρ_water and conclude that when ρ_block < ρ_water, the buoyant force exceeds weight, so the block would float without the string. The reasoning that the string must therefore pull downward (anchor below) is a direct consequence of the density comparison and equilibrium condition. This is Unit 8-specific content; without Unit 8, a student cannot reason through the density-dependent conclusion.

uncertainty_flags: Unit 8 (Fluids) has zero released-exam FRQ-level misconception or scoring data in the 2024/2026 sources reviewed in the fact pack (Chief Reader Report, Scoring Guidelines, Q1/Q2 Sample Responses, both released FRQ booklets). This item is the first Fluids FRQ in the Cramapple corpus and should be treated as lower-confidence for misconception patterns until a released-exam Fluids item appears. The CED content (Archimedes' principle, buoyant force, equilibrium) is solid and primary-source-verified, but real student-response scoring patterns are not yet available.

The rubric's treatment of part (a) tension direction is ambiguous: the canonical answer shows that tension direction depends on anchor location (determined in part b), but the criterion specifies 'tension acting downward' as the only acceptable direction in part (a). This creates a logical sequencing issue—a student who correctly reasons through both configurations in part (a) and then correctly eliminates the upward-anchor case in part (b) may be penalized in part (a) for not pre-committing to the downward direction. Recommend clarifying whether part (a) should accept tension direction as 'to be determined' or whether the rubric intends a single-path solution.

The criterion for part (b) requires the formula T=(ρ_water−ρ_block)gV but does not specify whether algebraic derivation from ΣF=0 is required or whether stating it with the density reasoning is sufficient. The canonical answer shows derivation; the rubric criterion does not. Recommend clarifying the derivation expectation.

No explicit statement in the rubric about follow-through/error-carried-forward credit: if a student makes an error in part (a) (e.g., wrong tension direction), can they still earn full credit on part (b) if their reasoning there is sound? The fact pack documents that Physics 1 scoring allows follow-through credit (e.g., 2024 Q1 sample response with wrong height but full downstream credit), but this rubric does not address it. Recommend adding a note.

scope_violation.evidence: All content falls within Units 5 and 6 scope: rotational inertia (5.4), rolling without slipping (6.5), rotational kinetic energy (6.1), and conservation of energy applied to rolling systems (6.5). No calculus, no vector cross products, no elliptical orbits, no viscosity or Bernoulli flow. Solid sphere vs. thin shell comparison is a standard qualitative/quantitative translation archetype.

criterion_units.evidence: Criterion requires comparison of I/(MR²) values for two objects of equal mass and radius. This is direct application of Unit 5.4 (Rotational Inertia): 'A rigid system's rotational inertia in a given plane is minimized when the axis passes through the system's center of mass' and the qualitative principle that 'rotational inertia is greater when mass is farther from the axis of rotation, which is why a hoop has more rotational inertia than a solid disk of the same mass and radius.' The solid sphere has mass distributed closer to the axis than a thin shell, so I_sphere < I_shell for equal M and R.

Criterion requires linking rotational inertia to translational acceleration via energy reasoning. This is Unit 6.1 (Rotational Kinetic Energy) and 6.5 (Rolling): 'Total KE of a rigid system = rotational KE about its center of mass + translational KE of the center of mass.' For a rolling object, gravitational PE is split between K_trans and K_rot. Smaller I means less energy goes into rotation at a given ω, leaving more for translational motion, hence greater a_cm. This energy-split reasoning is the core of Unit 6 content.

Criterion requires deriving v² = 2gh/[1 + I/(MR²)] from conservation of energy for rolling without slipping. This is Unit 6.5 (Rolling): 'K_tot = K_trans + K_rot' and 'rolling without slipping: v_cm = rω.' Starting from mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω² and substituting ω = v/r yields mgh = ½mv²(1 + I/(MR²)), so v² = 2gh/[1 + I/(MR²)]. This is the canonical rolling-energy formula for Unit 6. The comparison of two objects at the same height h directly applies this formula to show v_sphere > v_shell because I_sphere/(MR²) < I_shell/(MR²).

uncertainty_flags: The canonical answer for (a) combines prediction and reason into a single statement ('The solid sphere has smaller I/(MR²), so it accelerates more...'). The rubric splits this into two separate 1-point criteria. Verify that the rubric intends both points to be earned from a single, well-reasoned response, or clarify whether (a-prediction) and (a-reason) are meant to be earned independently (e.g., a student could earn (a-prediction) by correctly naming the sphere without earning (a-reason) if they fail to justify via rotational inertia).

Criterion (b-speed) asks for 'final translational speed' comparison and cites the formula v² = 2gh/[1 + I/(MR²)]. The rubric does not explicitly require students to show that both objects fall the same height h, or to state that h cancels in the ratio v_sphere/v_shell. Clarify whether a student who correctly applies the formula but does not explicitly invoke 'same height' earns full credit, or whether that step is a separate evidence requirement.

The stem says 'roll without slipping from rest down the same incline' but does not specify the incline angle or length. The formula v² = 2gh depends only on vertical drop h, not on incline geometry. Verify that the canonical answer's use of h (not arc length or angle) is intentional and that students are expected to recognize this independence.

scope_violation.evidence: The item assesses rotational equilibrium (Unit 5.5), force balance (Unit 2.4), torque calculation (Unit 5.3), and center-of-mass location (Unit 2.1) — all core Physics 1 content. The experimental design (part a, c) is a standard Experimental Design and Analysis FRQ archetype. No calculus, no vector cross products, no multi-plane rotation, no non-ideal springs or friction models appear.

criterion_units.evidence: Criterion requires identifying equilibrium data (force measurement, support locations, stick mass). Unit 2.1 (center of mass) and Unit 2.4 (force equilibrium, ΣF=0) are both required to set up the measurement. Unit 5.5 (rotational equilibrium) frames the overall experimental context.

Criterion requires applying vertical force balance ΣF=0 to infer the unmeasured support force. This is Unit 2.4 (Newton's First Law in translational form). A student who has not covered Unit 2 cannot earn this point.

Criterion requires choosing a support as the torque pivot to make its own force's lever arm zero. This is a direct application of Unit 5.3 (torque definition and lever-arm concept) and Unit 5.5 (rotational equilibrium, Στ=0). A student unfamiliar with torque and lever arms cannot execute this step.

Criterion requires writing the torque balance equation F₂(x₂−x₁)=mg(x_cm−x₁) with correct lever arms and applying Στ=0. This is Unit 5.3 (torque magnitude τ=rF_⊥) and Unit 5.5 (rotational equilibrium). A student without Unit 5 cannot derive or apply this equation.

Criterion requires verifying that the computed center-of-mass location falls between the two support locations (20–80 cm) and reproduces both force and torque balances. This requires understanding both Unit 2.1 (center of mass must lie within the support region for a supported object) and Unit 5.5 (rotational equilibrium check). A student without both units cannot perform this consistency check meaningfully.

Criterion requires designing a replication strategy (moving supports to different locations, averaging results) to reduce measurement uncertainty. While this is a general experimental-design skill, the specific context (changing support geometry while keeping the stick unchanged, then averaging center-of-mass estimates) requires understanding that the center of mass is an intrinsic property of the stick (Unit 2.1) and that torque equilibrium will hold at any support configuration (Unit 5.5). A student without Unit 5 cannot reason about why this replication strategy is valid.

uncertainty_flags: The canonical answer for criterion c-check specifies 'between the two actual support locations (20 cm and 80 cm) — not merely somewhere between 0 and 100 cm on the meterstick.' This is a subtle but important distinction: the center of mass must lie between the two *supports*, not just on the stick. The rubric evidence requirement captures this correctly, but a student might misinterpret 'between the support locations' as 'anywhere on the stick' if not carefully coached. The minimum fix ('Substitute the result back into force and torque balance, and check it against the 20-80 cm support bounds specifically') is clear and should prevent this ambiguity.

Criterion a-infer requires the student to state or apply F₁+F₂=mg. The canonical answer uses the notation F₁ = mg − F₂, which is algebraically equivalent but requires the student to recognize that the two support forces are the only vertical forces. A student might instead write ΣF=0 without explicitly naming the two forces, or might forget to include the stick's weight. The minimum fix ('Include the stick's weight in vertical balance') addresses this, but the evidence requirement could be more explicit: 'Applies F₁+F₂=mg or equivalent form, explicitly including the stick's weight mg.'

Criterion b-torque uses the equation F₂(x₂−x₁)=mg(x_cm−x₁). This assumes the student has chosen support 1 as the pivot. If the student chooses support 2 as the pivot instead, the equation becomes F₁(x₂−x₁)=mg(x₂−x_cm), which is equally valid. The evidence requirement states 'Correct lever arms and torque balance' but does not explicitly acknowledge this symmetry. A rubric scorer should accept either pivot choice as long as the lever arms and torque balance are correct.

The item does not specify whether the stick is uniform or nonuniform in the stem, but the stimulus states 'A nonuniform meterstick.' This is correct and necessary (a uniform stick's center of mass would be at 50 cm by symmetry, making the experiment trivial). However, the canonical answer does not explicitly state that the nonuniformity is the reason the experiment is necessary. A student might not recognize why this experiment is needed if they assume the stick is uniform. The rubric should clarify that the nonuniformity is given and that the experiment is designed to locate the unknown center of mass.

Criterion c-uncertainty requires 'a concrete replication strategy.' The canonical answer specifies 'repeat the measurement with the supports moved to different locations along the stick, and average the resulting (compatible) center-of-mass estimates from each configuration.' This is concrete, but a student might instead propose repeating the measurement at the same support locations multiple times and averaging, which would reduce random measurement error but not systematic error. The rubric should clarify that 'different support locations' is the intended strategy, not just repeated measurements at the same locations. The minimum fix ('Change support geometry while keeping the stick unchanged') addresses this, but the evidence requirement could be more explicit.

findings: All 8 criteria are present and point-specific.
Criteria are ordered logically: part (a) qualitative + quantitative (3 pts), part (b) two-system energy calculation (3 pts), part (c) period independence + physical reasoning (2 pts).
Each criterion specifies evidence requirements that are checkable and distinct.
Minimum fixes are actionable and map to the evidence requirements.
No criterion conflates multiple independent skills into a single point.

scope_violation.evidence: All content is within AP Physics 1 scope: energy conservation (Unit 3), simple harmonic motion (Unit 7), ideal spring systems (Unit 7.1-7.4), and amplitude-independence of period (Unit 7.3 explicit boundary: 'Changing the amplitude of an SHM system does not change its period'). No calculus, no nonideal springs, no damping, no external driving forces.

criterion_units.evidence: Qualitative comparison of K vs. U at a specific position within an oscillation requires understanding energy distribution in SHM (Unit 7.4: 'K is maximum when U is minimum and vice versa') and conservation of energy (Unit 3.4). The position x=A/2 is not at an extremum, so both K and U are nonzero; determining which is larger requires Unit 3 energy-conservation reasoning applied to Unit 7 oscillator context.

Evaluating total energy E=(1/2)kA² (Unit 7.4: 'For a spring-object system specifically: E_total=(1/2)kA²') and spring potential energy U=(1/2)k(Δx)² (Unit 3.3: 'Spring: U_s=(1/2)k(Δx)²') at x=A/2 requires both Unit 3 PE formalism and Unit 7 oscillator energy structure.
Deriving K=E-U from conservation of energy (Unit 3.4: 'E_total=K+U; conservation of energy...') and concluding K>U is a direct application of Unit 3 energy conservation to a Unit 7 oscillator.

Writing the energy-conservation equation (1/2)kA²=(1/2)k(A/2)²+(1/2)mv² requires Unit 3.4 conservation of energy and Unit 7.4 total-energy structure for a spring-mass system. A student who has not covered Unit 3 cannot set up this equation.

Solving for v_1=(A/2)√(3k/m) requires algebraic manipulation of the Unit 3 energy equation and extraction of speed from kinetic energy (Unit 3.1: 'K=(1/2)mv²'). Unit 3 is required to interpret the kinetic-energy term.

Applying the same energy-conservation method to the second system with amplitude 2A at position x=A (the analogous half-amplitude point) requires Unit 3 energy conservation and Unit 7 understanding that the period is amplitude-independent (so the two systems can be compared at corresponding phases). The scaling relationship v_2=2v_1 emerges from Unit 3 energy algebra applied to Unit 7 oscillators.

Stating that the period T=2π√(m/k) is independent of amplitude is a direct statement of Unit 7.3 boundary condition: 'Changing the amplitude of an SHM system does not change its period.' A student who has not covered Unit 7 cannot know this fact.

Explaining *why* amplitude independence holds requires reasoning about the trade-off between distance traveled and speed at each phase (Unit 7.3: 'Properties of SHM can be determined and analyzed graphically' and Unit 7.4 energy structure). The physical reasoning that 'increased distance and increased speed offset each other exactly' is a Unit 7 conceptual claim grounded in Unit 3 energy scaling: if amplitude doubles, total energy quadruples (E ∝ A²), so speeds at corresponding phases double (v ∝ A), exactly offsetting the doubled path length.

uncertainty_flags: Part (b) criterion-03 assumes the student recognizes that x=A (for amplitude 2A) is the 'analogous half-amplitude position' to x=A/2 (for amplitude A). This is a valid comparison, but the rubric does not explicitly require the student to state this correspondence. A student might instead evaluate the second system at x=2A/2=A without explicitly naming it as 'half-amplitude,' and the rubric as written would still award the point if v_2=A√(3k/m) is obtained. This is acceptable (the evidence requirement is met), but the rubric could be more explicit about the position correspondence if precision is desired.

Part (c) criterion-02 asks for 'physical reasoning' beyond formula citation, but does not specify a minimum depth. The canonical answer provides a clear mechanism (distance and speed scale together), but a student might instead reason qualitatively (e.g., 'the cart moves faster with larger amplitude, so it covers the extra distance in the same time') without deriving the exact scaling. The rubric should clarify whether such a qualitative explanation suffices or whether the scaling relationship must be made explicit.

The rubric does not explicitly penalize dimensional errors or sign errors in part (b), though the evidence requirement 'The algebra and square root are correct' could be interpreted to include dimensional consistency. Confirm whether a student who writes v_1=(A/2)√(3k/m) with incorrect units (e.g., forgetting to simplify √(k/m) to √(k/m)) would lose the point or receive follow-through credit.

findings: All three criteria are present and point-valued.
